content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of rapid drug susceptibility testing (DST) for isoniazid and rifampicin, or rifampicin alone, over conventional testing or no testing at the time of tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, depending on available resources. For monitoring patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) during treatment, sputum smear microscopy combined with culture is preferred over sputum smear microscopy alone. Anti-TB drugs are categorized into groups based on their efficacy, usage experience, and drug class. First-line anti-TB drugs are classified under Group 1, except for streptomycin, which is grouped with other injectable agents in Group 2. Drugs in Groups 2–5, excluding streptomycin, are considered second-line or reserve drugs. Cross-resistance mutations in Mycobacterium tuberculosis can lead to resistance to other drugs within the same family and, less commonly, to drugs in different groups. WHO guidelines for MDR-TB treatment recommend the inclusion of a fluoroquinolone and ethionamide (or prothionamide) as part of the regimen, despite the evidence being of very low quality. Later-generation fluoroquinolones are preferred over earlier-generation ones. During the intensive phase of treatment, at least four second-line drugs likely to be effective, including a parenteral agent and pyrazinamide, should be used. Regimens should include pyrazinamide, a fluoroquinolone, a parenteral agent, ethionamide (or prothionamide), and either cycloserine or para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) if cycloserine cannot be used. Major changes in second-line anti-TB regimens for MDR-TB include the recommendation to use at least four effective second-line drugs along with pyrazinamide during the intensive phase. There is no evidence supporting the use of more than four second-line drugs in patients with extensive disease, but additional drugs may be included if the effectiveness of some drugs is uncertain. Ethambutol and Group 5 drugs may be used but are not part of the standard regimen. In cases of culture-negative pulmonary TB with radiographic evidence of prior TB, the inability to isolate M. tuberculosis does not exclude active TB. Alternative diagnoses should be carefully considered, and further diagnostic studies should be conducted. A diagnosis of TB can be inferred from clinical and radiographic responses to anti-TB treatment. Reevaluation after two months of therapy is essential to assess treatment response. If clinical or radiographic improvement is observed and no other etiology is identified, treatment should continue for active TB. Standard regimens include six-month chemotherapy or a four-month regimen of isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RIF), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB) for two months, followed by INH and RIF for an additional two months. HIV-infected patients with culture-negative pulmonary TB should be treated for at least six months. For pregnant women, TB treatment should begin when the probability of maternal disease is moderate to high. The initial regimen should include INH, RIF, and EMB, as these drugs cross the placenta but are not teratogenic. Streptomycin is contraindicated due to its association with congenital deafness. PZA is likely safe during pregnancy and is recommended by WHO and the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD). If PZA is excluded, therapy should last a minimum of nine months. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated for women on first-line anti-TB drugs, as the drug concentrations in breast milk are not toxic to the infant. However, these drugs in breast milk are not sufficient to treat TB or latent TB infection in the infant. Pyridoxine supplementation (25 mg/day) is recommended for all women taking INH during pregnancy or breastfeeding. In low-income countries, the rise in HIV infections and neglect of TB control programs have contributed to a resurgence of TB, including drug-resistant strains. Between 2000 and 2004, 20% of TB cases were resistant to standard treatments, and 2% were resistant to second-line drugs. TB incidence varies widely due to differences in healthcare systems. WHO declared TB a global health emergency in 1993, and the Stop TB Partnership developed a Global Plan to save 14 million lives between 2006 and 2015. Understanding TB treatment approaches in high-incidence, low-income countries is essential for applying international guidelines effectively. The WHO and IUATLD guidelines target countries with limited access to mycobacterial culture, drug susceptibility testing, radiographic facilities, and second-line drugs. The WHO and IUATLD recommend standardized eight-month regimens for patients who have relapsed, interrupted treatment, or failed treatment. Patients failing supervised retreatment are considered chronic cases and are likely to have MDR-TB. Susceptibility testing and tailored regimens using second-line drugs are recommended if resources are available. Neither baseline nor follow-up biochemical testing is recommended. Patients should be educated to recognize and report symptoms of drug toxicity promptly. New pharmacotherapy advances include the FDA-approved drug bedaquiline for MDR-TB, which carries a black-box warning for arrhythmias. A novel three-drug regimen (PaMZ) consisting of PA-824, moxifloxacin, and pyrazinamide has shown promise in killing over 99% of TB bacteria within two weeks in clinical trials. Research is ongoing to develop new drugs to shorten treatment duration, improve MDR-TB therapy, and enhance latent TB infection management. Promising drug classes include nitroimidazopyrans and oxazolidinones. Experimental data suggest that inhibiting isocitrate lyase, an enzyme necessary for latent TB, may be useful. Other interventions, such as drug delivery systems, cytokine inhibitors, protective cytokines, and nutritional supplements, require further investigation. Identifying factors predictive of relapse risk and therapy adherence could optimize resource allocation and treatment outcomes.
